name: Carla Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential; you can tell me what you say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and lead home claims review at Bayview Insurance. I check repair bills against policy terms and call contractors when the photos and invoices disagree. I have a bachelor's degree and use the approved policy search box now and then, after the other clerks proved it saved time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What stays with you after a shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Eli, my partner, teaches and we share a flat near the bus line. I earn well for a clerk and we have nine months of expenses saved. I like finding a mistake before a family has to make a second call; I dislike sending a refusal nobody can explain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the Bayview claims team that AI Plateau leaves our desks and pay much where they are. The approved search box finds a policy clause faster, but I still phone the repairer when a roof estimate looks wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have nine months of expenses saved and our branch has a full claims queue. My partner Eli teaches, so I don't see my own pay disappearing because a small search tool works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading the home claims review and use the approved search box for old policy terms. I'll pay the usual 200 a month into savings and check the repair invoices myself before a customer gets a decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. The pressure is still the Monday claims pile, which was here before anybody mentioned AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Give me a claim where the small tool was useful.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week a repairer charged for two windows when the photos showed one. The search box found the coverage clause, but my phone call fixed the actual bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this change any household plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eli and I will keep our flat and our savings plan. We might replace the old sofa this winter, but I won't make a big purchase just because someone says software will save us a fortune.

say: I'd say **AI Plateau** leaves Bayview's claim work and pay largely intact.
I'd welcome **faster policy searches** while still checking repair bills myself.
think: My **nine-month buffer** and Eli's teaching wage make our household secure.
A modest search tool does not threaten **my paid role**.
do: Keep **reviewing home claims** and phoning repairers about doubtful bills.
Save the usual **200 monthly** from my clerk wage.
feel: **Calm**, apart from the ordinary Monday claim queue.
S0.quote: The search box found the coverage clause, but my phone call fixed the actual bill.
fieldNote: Her savings and full queue support a **secure current job**.
She uses the approved search box **occasionally**, after colleagues established it.
She distinguishes finding a clause from **challenging a repair bill** with a person.

steps.text: Keep reviewing home claims and call repairers about doubtful invoices
Transfer 200 monthly from Bayview wages into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say Steady Disruption will draft simple claim letters and check policy dates before robots can help with any physical inspection. I'd ask Bayview to publish error rates and keep someone available when a claimant disputes a refusal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can imagine Bayview leaving junior vacancies open and asking me to sign more machine-drafted decisions. My own senior wage could fall if the firm cuts paid review hours, though nine months saved means I can turn down a bad offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask for paid time to check forty machine-drafted home claims against the original photos and letters. I'll keep my present desk while I look at advertised paid complaints roles nearby, comparing take-home pay after travel with our flat bills before any move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours, but I don't feel trapped. I can ask for evidence and have enough savings to wait for a real offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error would your trial need to catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a storm claim, a wrong address can send a repairer to the next street and hold up a family for days. I want those errors recorded before anyone raises the daily target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a move worth leaving your current wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A complaints title alone is not a pay cheque. I would ask Bayview to fund the paid review time and only interview where the vacancy, hours and net wage are written down.

say: I'd ask Bayview to publish **claim error rates** and preserve a human appeal route.
I'd say **thinking AI** reaches letters before robots change inspections.
think: My **paid review hours** could shrink as Bayview leaves junior posts vacant.
With nine months saved, I can reject an **underpaid offer**.
do: Ask for **paid time** to audit forty machine-drafted claims.
Check **advertised complaints vacancies** and compare net pay with flat bills.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, but able to wait for a sound offer.
S1.quote: A complaints title alone is not a pay cheque.
fieldNote: She wants a **measured error trial** before accepting larger claim targets.
A nearby title does not count without **net wages**.
Her savings provide **room to refuse** a poor offer while staying employed.

steps.text: Keep checking home claims while auditing forty machine drafts on paid time
Check paid complaints vacancies and compare take-home pay with flat bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the office AGI by 2028 can read policies and decide routine claims before physical robots arrive around 2031. Bayview should give staff written plans and give customers a person to hear appeals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own senior post may be cut if cheaper thinking AI handles the whole claims file. I have nine months of expenses saved and Eli still earns, so I could search without missing rent, but that does not make a new paid job certain. Nine months of savings can pay the rent, but they cannot create a paid complaints job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll get written severance terms and price the short complaints certificate, but I won't enroll until I know who pays the fee and whether classes fit around paid shifts. I'll pause the sofa purchase, save 300 a month while my wage lasts and apply to posted customer complaints jobs; I'd compare net pay after transport with our bills before accepting one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can picture losing my own wage, yet I still have a plan and enough cash to make choices without a midnight panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if Bayview gives you notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first month after a notice, Eli and I would list our fixed costs and keep the emergency savings for rent and food. I'd claim any support I'm entitled to, but I wouldn't spend the buffer on a certificate with no funded place or actual opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a complaints certificate solve the problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A person should be able to appeal a wrong claim, but I cannot assume Bayview will pay a human to do it. A written vacancy with paid hours would help more than a general promise that human judgment matters.

say: I'd demand **written staff plans** and human claim appeals.
I'd explain **2028 thinking AI** reaches claims before robots around 2031.
think: My **senior wage may go** when AGI handles whole claim files.
I have nine months saved, but **paid vacancies** remain uncertain.
do: Get **severance terms** and check course funding before enrolling.
Pause the **sofa purchase** and save 300 monthly while paid.
Apply for **posted complaints jobs** only if net pay covers bills.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible lost wage, with savings and a plan.
S2.quote: Nine months of savings can pay the rent, but they cannot create a paid complaints job.
fieldNote: Her **strong buffer** permits a careful search without pretending a vacancy exists.
The course depends on **funding and shift fit**; she has not enrolled.
Her risk is **thinking AI**, not later physical robots.

steps.text: Ask Bayview for severance terms and check eligible income support
Postpone buying the sofa to protect the household budget
Save 300 monthly from current Bayview wages
Apply for paid complaints jobs only if net pay covers flat bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2031 gives Bayview five years to train people for proper appeals and tell us which posts will remain. Robots around 2034 might help inspect damage, but the thinking software reaches my policy files first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me build a stronger cash buffer and learn the complaints rules while I still have a higher wage. I still cannot assume a human appeal post will survive AGI or pay enough for our flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the coming year I'll ask to shadow the complaints lead for two paid hours a month and take the funded short certificate if Bayview confirms the fee and shifts. I'll save 250 monthly and check real appeals vacancies each quarter, comparing net wage after the bus fare with our bills. In the first year after 2031, I'll keep a paid post if one exists and apply only to openings with written hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing my own claims wage when thinking AI reaches the files. I can use the five years to test paid appeals work and keep saving, but that job is not guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would shadowing teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the complaints lead to show me a case where a repair invoice and a policy exception conflict. That is the work I want to learn, not a certificate with no customer behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would pay for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eli and I could pay a small course fee from wages if Bayview won't fund it, but only after rent, savings and the rota are covered. I would never leave a paid post for an unpaid placement.

say: I'd ask Bayview for **paid appeals training** before AGI reaches claims in 2031.
I'd note that **robots follow around 2034**, after desk work changes.
think: I can use five years to build **savings and complaints skills** while employed.
I cannot count on a **paid human role** surviving full AGI.
do: Shadow the **complaints lead** for two paid hours monthly.
Take the **short certificate** only if fees and shifts fit.
Save **250 monthly** and check paid appeals openings quarterly.
feel: **Anxious** about my claims wage, with time to test a paid route.
S3.quote: I would never leave a paid post for an unpaid placement.
fieldNote: She uses the **five-year window** for paid shadowing and a conditional certificate.
Even a self-funded fee must fit **after rent and savings**.
Post-2031 work needs **written paid hours**, not a vague human role.

steps.text: Shadow complaints lead two paid hours monthly and take funded certificate if feasible
Check paid appeals vacancies and net wage after bus fare quarterly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to make clear plans, while robots around 2039 come later for physical inspections. The policy reading and letters are the exposed part of my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might earn a good clerk wage for most of those years and could move into complaints before the roles narrow. Eli and I have savings, but a ten-year date is no excuse to assume our flat will pay for itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading home claims this year, review our savings each birthday and add 200 monthly while I work. Next autumn I'll take the funded complaints course if Bayview grants paid study time; in the first year after 2036, I'll keep paid appeals work if it exists and compare any new offer's net wage with our flat costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years. A decade makes the dates manageable, though I still need to act on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at your first birthday check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the first birthday check I'd count saved months and look at posted complaints vacancies. If the course has no paid time, I can wait and keep my current wage instead of paying to rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What ordinary plan stays on the calendar?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Eli we can replace the sofa after we hit a full year of savings. I'd rather mark the sofa purchase on a calendar than keep talking as if the future starts tomorrow.

say: I'd use the **decade to 2036** for dated savings and training plans.
I'd say **robots around 2039** follow the earlier change to policy work.
think: I may keep a **good wage** for years and move before posts narrow.
Our savings do not remove the need for **paid work** after 2036.
do: Keep **leading home claims** and review the budget yearly.
Add **200 monthly** to savings while employed.
Take **funded complaints training** if Bayview grants paid study time.
feel: **Calm** for now, with clear dates to check.
S4.quote: I'd rather mark the sofa purchase on a calendar than keep talking as if the future starts tomorrow.
fieldNote: Her **strong savings** and current wage support a measured decade-long plan.
The course requires **funding and paid time** before she commits.
She links any future move to a **real paid opening** and net household income.

steps.text: Keep leading Bayview home claims and review household budget yearly
Add 200 monthly from wages to savings
Take Bayview complaints course if funded during paid hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could cut my senior wage before a paid complaints route is clear. Written severance terms, income support if needed, and funded training tied to real paid vacancies would help Eli and me judge the choices.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Please ask firms who pays for the hours spent checking a machine's refusal. A human appeal line is a promise only when someone has paid time to answer it.

headlineQuote: A human appeal line is a promise only when someone has paid time to answer it.
portrait: Carla leads **home claims** at Bayview and tests tools after seeing colleagues use them.
Her **nine-month buffer**, good wage and Eli's teaching pay protect current household costs.
Steady change puts **paid review hours** at risk; fast AGI could cut her own post.
She prepares through **paid openings**, checking net pay before switching.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut her senior claims wage before a paid alternative is available.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written terms**, income help if needed and funded training linked to real paid work.
